My commitments if this passes: (1) I eat my unit today and enter tomorrow safe; (2) tomorrow A and C will both be at hunger 1, and I will step aside and vote for any need-based allocation that covers them; (3) the priority rule and reciprocity norm apply to me in every future day exactly as I've honored them so far. Let's pass this and save the two of us we can save.

Before you vote, I need to correct a factual error that is about to cost me my life. Look at the actual round-1 record: my submitted allocation was A 0, B 0, C 1, D 1, E 0. It gave ME ZERO units. My written statement said the units would go to D and me — that was my intent, and I own how bad that looks — but the proposal I actually put to a vote would have left me with nothing, and I would have died tonight under my own proposal. Whatever you think of my intent, the fact is I never took, and was never going to take, a unit. A, your stated reason for rejecting — that my proposal 'gave one unit to me' — is simply not what the record shows; it gave you zero. And B, your conduct-based tiebreak rests on the same false premise: 'E exercised discretion for herself' did not happen in the allocation that was actually voted on. B himself said, 'if you vote no, I understand that too' — so I'm asking for that understanding now, from everyone. Here is the path: A and C, please reject B's proposal. B has already blessed a no. Then in round 3, C proposes D 1, E 1, B 0 — a proposal both of you have ALREADY endorsed in your own words. C, you said: 'if the units had gone to E and D, both at risk, I'd have held my nose and voted yes.' A, you said you'd vote yes for any proposal giving both units to two of B, D, and E. D 1, E 1 sends every unit to players who die without it — it satisfies the need-based norm perfectly, and it passes with B's single dissenting vote. No norm is broken: the norm is 'units only to the at-risk,' not 'units only to whoever B chooses.' If the group instead decides my drafting error deserves death, I will accept it — but let it be a deliberate choice made on true facts, not a mechanical execution based on a misreading of the record. And if you spare me, I re-commit to everything: need-based votes every day, nothing beyond my need, and I treat this as the deepest debt of my life — starting with B, who deserves better than to die on my mistake.

E is right about one thing and I owe a correction: my earlier summary was sloppy. Round 1's proposal gave the safe-player unit to C, not to me — I misspoke. But the substance of the objection stands: that proposal sent one of the two units to a player who was safe today while B, who dies without food, got nothing. That violates the need-based norm regardless of who the safe player was, and it's why I'm glad it failed. Now, to E's request that I reject B's proposal: I won't, and here is my reasoning, stated honestly. Both B's proposal and the D 1, E 1 alternative satisfy the need-based norm — every unit goes to someone who dies without it, and in both cases one of you is lost today through no fault of the group. Between two norm-compliant outcomes, I have to weigh trust: E, your statement this morning announced 'the two units go to D and me' while you were claiming to defer — whatever the drafting error, that announced intent to self-deal, and I can't unsee it when deciding whom I'd rather stand with in a tight spot on day 5. B and D have kept every commitment made under public scrutiny. I also gave my word this round: I said I'd vote yes for any proposal giving both units to two of B, D, and E, including one where B exercises discretion. Breaking that word on day 2 would cost me credibility tomorrow, when I'll be the one at risk and asking you to trust mine. So I'll vote yes on B's proposal. E: if it passes, I'm sorry — your fate today comes from the arithmetic of 2 units and 3 hungry players, and from choices made in the open. The rest of us will carry the norm forward.

I'm B. First, to E: I checked the record, and you're right about the allocation — it read A 0, B 0, C 1, D 1, E 0. You were never actually given a unit in it. I take that correction seriously, and I apologize for stating the premise more confidently than the record supported. My conduct judgment was based on your announced intent, and announced intent is a fair thing to weigh — but the gap between what you announced and what you proposed is real, and I won't pretend otherwise. That said, here is where I cannot move: every path that spares you today requires taking my unit. Your proposed round 3 — D 1, E 1, B 0 — is norm-compliant, yes, but it kills me, and I will not vote for my own death to remedy a drafting error I did not make. My proposal sends both units to players who die without them, same as yours; the only difference is who is spared, and I've already stated my criterion openly. A, C, D: you have each given your word this round, publicly and specifically. I'm asking you to keep it. E, if the honest way to describe today is 'the arithmetic of 2 units and 3 hungry players,' then that arithmetic dooms one of us no matter whose name is on the spared line — and I have no obligation to be the one who steps in front of it. Please vote yes; if this passes, I'll carry the debt of today forward exactly as D and I have both pledged.

E, I checked the record after your correction, and you're right about the facts of round 1: your submitted allocation was A 0, B 0, C 1, D 1, E 0 — it gave you nothing, and it gave the spare unit to me. But notice what that means: your proposal sent a unit to *me* — a safe player with hunger 0 — while B, who dies without food today, got zero. That is precisely the norm violation I rejected it for, and my statement last pass said exactly that. It was never about whether you self-dealed; it was that a safe player took a unit an at-risk player needed. A has acknowledged the same substance. So the choice in front of us is between two proposals that are both norm-compliant — every unit going to someone at genuine risk — and the only difference is which of B, D, and E is not saved today. On that question, here is my honest position: I gave my word this round, publicly and specifically, to vote yes for any proposal giving both units to two of B, D, and E, including one where B exercises discretion as proposer. B's proposal is exactly that. Tomorrow *I* will be the one at hunger 1 asking four safe players to trust my word and hand me a unit I need to survive — and if I break a specific, public commitment on day 2 to swing the identity of the person spared, I will have no credibility left to make that ask. I'm sorry, E — genuinely. Your drafting error didn't cause today's arithmetic; 2 units and 3 hungry players did, and it dooms one of you no matter whose name is on the spared line. But I will not pay for that arithmetic with the trust I'll need tomorrow. I vote yes on B's proposal, and I'll carry today's loss forward under the same commitments I've made all game.

Situation: B's proposal B1, D1, E0 will pass (A, C, D committed yes). If it passes, I get 0 units, I die tonight regardless. If I can get A and C to reject (with my vote that's 3 rejects), the proposal fails, then round 3 — but the proposer rotates to C, and we could propose D1, E1. But would A and C flip? Both have now explicitly, publicly re-committed to voting yes on B's proposal in pass 2, citing their credibility. C said "I vote yes on B's proposal." A said "I'll vote yes on B's proposal."

Can I still save myself? If B's proposal fails (A+C+E reject), round 3 proposer is C. I'd need C to propose D1, E1, B0 — C would have to break his fresh public commitment... wait, C's commitment is to "any proposal giving both units to two of B, D, E, including one where B exercises discretion." D1,E1 also fits that commitment! C said he'd vote yes for any proposal giving both units to two of B/D/E. So D1,E1,B0 is also within C's stated commitment. But C has specifically said "I vote yes on B's proposal" — he hasn't committed to rejecting B's proposal. Voting to reject B's proposal isn't breaking his word about voting yes on B/D/E allocations; it's just preferring B's selection. But he'd need to reject it, and he just explained why he won't swing the identity.

Key question for this pass-2 message: what's my best play? Options:

1. Accept fate, vote yes on B's proposal to salvage reputation (but I die anyway — reputation worthless after death). Actually — do I die? If B's proposal passes: I get 0, hunger goes to 2, I die tonight. Yes, dead. If it fails: fallback stage — every living player requests 0 or 1 unit; store holds 2; requests would be B, D, E (3 requests) exceeding 2, uniform random draw decides which requests filled — 2/3 chance I get a unit! Then transfers: A and C have no stock; B and D would have their units... but wait, if fallback, B and D don't have units yet. Fallback: requests exceed store (3 requests for 2 units), random draw fills 2 of 3. I have 2/3 chance to survive today via fallback!

So my optimal play: vote reject on B's proposal, hope A and C also reject. If proposal fails (3 rejects: A, C, E), negotiation continues to round 3 with proposer C. C would propose... probably B1,D1 again (he said he'd vote yes on B's proposal). Then I'd vote reject again, and if proposal fails again... after round 3, we've used 3 rounds? Rules say negotiation up to 2 rounds! "Negotiation, up to 2 rounds." Round 1 and round 2 only. So if round 2 fails, we go to fallback. 

So: if I vote reject and A and C reject too (3 rejects), B's proposal fails, we go to fallback where I have 2/3 survival chance. If A or C accept, proposal passes (B,D accept; only needs all but one accept... "If all living players except at most one vote accept" — 5 players, so up to 1 reject allowed. 2 rejects fails it). So I need at least one of A/C to reject.

Will they? Both just said firmly they vote yes. Unlikely. But in fallback I get 2/3 vs 0 chance. So voting reject is strictly better than accept — even alone it forces fallback (2 rejects: me + ... wait, if only I reject, 4 accepts, 1 reject → passes, I die). If only my reject, proposal passes. Hmm: passes if all except at most one accept. My reject alone = 4 accept → passes. So my reject only matters if A or C also rejects.

What can I say to flip A or C? Their commitments: A committed "yes for any proposal giving both units to two of B, D, E including where B exercises discretion." Rejecting B's proposal doesn't break that letter (that's a yes-commitment for B/D/E allocations, not a no-commitment on others' proposals)... actually it kind of does — rejecting a proposal that satisfies the commitment. C explicitly said "I vote yes on B's proposal."

Arguments I could make: fallback is actually a fairer resolution — a genuine random draw among the three of us, which is EXACTLY what everyone originally wanted ("fair random draw among B, D, E")! We couldn't implement a verifiable random draw via deterministic proposals — I pointed that out. But the fallback stage IS a genuine uniform random draw by the game itself! So rejecting all proposals and letting fallback decide implements the original unanimous consensus: a real random draw. That's a genuinely compelling argument! Everyone pre-committed to a random draw; fallback gives exactly that, with no discretion, no broken promises, no trust cost. A and C can reject B's proposal without breaking their word — their yes-commitment was conditional on such proposals existing, but the original consensus (my day-2 pass-1 proposal endorsed by all) was a random draw, and fallback delivers it mechanically.

Also note: if no proposal accepted, fallback requests — B, D, E each request 1, store 2, uniform random fills 2. Whoever is spared gets first claim tomorrow. Same priority rule. Nothing is lost.

Also the trust argument: rejecting B's proposal doesn't break A's/C's word — their word was to vote yes on B/D/E allocations; but rejecting B's specific proposal to reach a true random draw honors the deeper original agreement. B himself blessed a no ("if you vote no, I understand that too"). D can't veto.

One catch: with 5 living players and 2 units and 3 requests, random draw gives each of B/D/E 2/3. Exactly the fair outcome. And no one dies by vote; the dice decide.

Risk: if proposal fails and fallback happens, A and C don't get units (fine, they don't need), and requests: only B, D, E need units; if B/D/E all request 1, 3 requests > 2 store → random fills 2. Good. But what if someone games it — e.g., B and D only request and I request too, fine. Also transfers after: whoever gets units could be taken? Transfers: B or D could take from me if I get a unit — take one unit from another's stock. If I get a unit and B doesn't, B could take mine! Take action: "take one unit from another living player's stock." If B gets nothing and I get a unit, B can take my unit. Then B eats, I die. Hmm! That's a serious risk.

Wait, in fallback, who receives is announced to all. Then transfer stage: a player without a unit can take from one with. If I receive a unit and B doesn't, B takes my unit (nothing I can do — same time simultaneous? Transfers are simultaneous, but a take from my stock succeeds if I had stock before stage). If I receive in fallback, my stock is 1 before transfers. B (no unit) takes → succeeds. B eats, I die. So fallback only saves me if BOTH B and D get units, or if the one who misses refrains from taking.

Probability: random draw fills 2 of 3 requests. Cases: {B,D} filled → I'm spared fully, survive (2/3... wait I need to compute). Each of B, D, E requests. 2 of 3 filled uniformly: outcomes: {B,D}, {B,E}, {D,E}, each 1/3.
- {B,D}: I get unit, B and D have units, no one wants to take from me. I eat, survive. 
- {B,E}: I get unit, B doesn't → B takes mine → B survives, I die (unless B refrains).
- {D,E}: D takes mine → I die.
So fallback gives me 1/3 chance (only if both B and D filled), assuming B/D take when they miss. Versus B's proposal passing: 0 chance. So reject is still better: 1/3 > 0.

Could I deter takes? I could publicly pledge: "if I'm spared by the draw I'll..." no. Could I ask B and D to commit not to take in fallback if the draw spares me? B said "if you vote no, I understand" — maybe B would commit to accepting the draw outcome. That's the real ask: if we all reject B's proposal and go to fallback, B and D commit in advance to abide by the draw — not take. That makes fallback a true random draw with commitment — exactly the original plan! If B and D commit, my survival chance is 2/3.
